description: I am a space engineering student with a passion for anything space related
summary:
AstroPulse is an offline, visual health tool that lets astronauts assess their own spine bone health during long missions and guides them on how to protect it. Astronauts lose 1-2% of bone density per month in microgravity, yet spine scans happen only before and after flight, so loss is found too late to act on.

It collects inputs the crew can take in space: monthly spine ultrasound, urine tests every 14 days, blood tests every 30 days, and daily back pain, exercise, food and medication logs. Color-coded charts show whether each indicator is in range, and a forecast shows where the spine is heading by landing. It never alerts from one noisy number. It escalates to flight surgeons only when several signals agree, and may advise exercise; medical related advise is done based on a doctor's diagnosis and analysis.

Ground doctors review every ultrasound and write notes that are uplinked back. Each reviewed scan, result and note is saved together as training data, so an AI model can learn to estimate spine density from ultrasound and improve with every mission. The AI estimate is a simulated concept today. A real model needs ultrasound scans paired with DXA results.

This matters for Moon and Mars missions and for remote communities far from specialists.
details:
Our project is an offline-first tablet app that helps an astronaut on a long mission, such as a trip to the Moon or Mars, check their own health and know what to do without waiting for Earth. Deep-space crews face communication delays of up to about 20 minutes each way and usually have no physician on board, so the astronaut is both the patient and the first responder. The app opens on bone health, the slowest and least visible risk on a long mission, and keeps general vitals on a separate Health tab. In Daily Mode, a 2-minute check-in compares each reading with the astronaut’s own 14-day space baseline instead of Earth textbook ranges, and labels it Normal, Watch or Act. A forecast shows where bone, heart, sleep and radiation dose are heading by mission end. A single odd reading triggers a re-measure prompt first, and the bone pattern alert fires only when several signals agree, such as exercise, urine NTx, scans, back pain and posture. Every status has a “Why?” panel that explains how spaceflight affects that indicator and cites the NASA or CSA source. If two vital signs leave their safe range together, Triage Mode switches to a full-screen Red Alert with numbered steps a non-doctor crewmate can follow, fully offline. A “Send to ground doctors” feature builds a downlink packet of scans, reports and biomarkers, and a hash-chained audit trail logs every reading, report and downlink.

The main benefit is early warning and prevention for people who launch healthy, rather than diagnosis. Personal baselines, the re-measure check and the multi-signal rule cut false alarms, while “how to measure” cards, plain-language explanations and a three-step plan (self-care, then the crew medical officer, then the flight surgeon) support astronauts who aren’t medical experts. The app works with no connection, uses transparent rules that can be explained and tested, and is designed for microgravity with large touch targets and status shown by labels and icons, not color alone. The intended impact is that crews on long missions catch problems like bone loss, blood pressure drift and radiation exposure early, act on them, and give ground doctors well-organized data at each comm window. Over time, the doctor-reviewed data builds the dataset needed to predict who will lose bone, which NASA says it can’t do today, and the same approach can serve remote and northern communities, people on long bed rest, and people with spinal cord injury.

We built the frontend with React 19, Vite and React Router, with custom dark high-contrast CSS, and Recharts for the charts. The engine is JavaScript that runs in the browser on bundled JSON data, with per-crew state in localStorage. An optional Node/Express mock API handles bone-health and trend analysis, and the app falls back to bundled data if it is unreachable. We used Python (NumPy and Pandas) to generate a reproducible, fixed-seed 180-day simulated mission for three crew members, since no public day-by-day in-flight vitals exist. Testing is done with Vitest, and the app is hosted on Firebase Hosting. Our data and evidence come from NASA’s Human Research Program, CSA’s radiation monitoring resources and NASA’s bed-rest DXA scans from study MR035G. No special hardware is needed because the app runs on any tablet or browser, and wearable feeds are simulated. Future work includes an anomaly-detection model exported to ONNX Runtime Web and offline Q&A with WebLLM.

The project is creative in how it turns data into action. It reads signals as a pattern against each astronaut’s own baseline rather than relying on single-number thresholds, and its forecast slider shows how the astronaut’s own choices, such as exercise, change the outcome. One app moves from calm daily coaching to a step-by-step emergency screen, which fits the idea that the astronaut is both patient and first responder. Doctors stay in charge, since every reviewed scan becomes training data for a future model.

Our team considered communication delays and offline use, so all logic runs locally and reports wait for the next comm window. We tagged every indicator with the NASA hazards that affect it, and we kept the tool descriptive: it gives no diagnoses, risk scores or medication advice. The in-flight crew data, the AI ultrasound estimate and the triage protocols are simulated or based on public sources, and the −2.5% watch level is team-chosen rather than a clinical threshold. We also accounted for data limits, since blood and urine markers are not direct measures of spine density and DXA can’t be done in flight, so those markers are only used together. Finally, we weighed usability for non-expert astronauts, trust through explainable rules and a tamper-evident audit trail, and a planned encrypted downlink.
